newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Expert sees BSE persisting, but low risk.
newsitem.headline: Expert sees BSE persisting, but low risk.

text.p: Mad cow disease will probably still be around five years from now, despite a British forecast to the contrary, but the risk will be very low, a leading international expert said on Wednesday.

Oxford University scientists forecast in August that the brain wasting disease, known as Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE), would die out by 2001 because the main cause of infection, contaminated feed, had been eliminated.
The report triggered the view in London that an extra cull of cattle, part of an agreement reached at an EU summit in Florence in June to defuse the crisis, was unnecessary.

But Professor Charles Weissmann of Zurich University, appointed last year by European Union Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler to chair a group of experts to fix BSE research priorities, said it was not clear the disease would disappear.

"I think it is pretty clear that it (mad cow disease) will diminish very considerably but whether it will go back to zero or whether there will be a low endemic level I don't think I would venture to predict," he told a news conference.
Weissmann called for more work on the transmission of BSE to humans and for development of a test for the disease on live animals and humans.
Speaking after presenting a report to Fischler, Weissmann said that there were doubts about the Oxford report but he declined to be drawn on whether Britain should carry out the extra cattle cull.
Britain last month shelved the cull of up to an extra 147,000 cattle most at risk to the disease, provoking a storm of protest from its EU partners.
Britain has already pledged to kill annually one million older cattle over 30 months of age and to burn the carcases to prevent the meat entering the human food chain.
"I am not quite sure that one can say that if all the sources of contaminated feed are eliminated that the disease will completely disappear," Weissmann said.
Animal feed containing ground-up meat and bone meal, is believed to be the main source of the disease.
But Weissmann said more research was needed into how the disease could be passed from cows to calves and whether there were any hidden infectious agents.
Asked whether he judged it safe to eat beef, Weissmann said: "I did go to Britain and did eat beef."
But he added, light-heartedly, that his judgement was influenced by his mature years and the long incubation period of the disease.
He said the evidence we have suggests that BSE could be passed to humans in the form of the deadly Creutzfeldt Jakob Disease (CJD) and we should assess that risk, he said.
BSE can also be transmitted orally to mice, cats, sheep and goats as well as to cattle. But more research was needed into whether pigs and chickens can catch the disease from eating infected feed.
Experiments should be carried out on similar species to humans, such as monkeys, by giving them them increasing amounts of infected feed, containing brain and other suspect tissue.
"The conclusion will not be definitive but it is the best we can do under the circumstances," Weissmann said.
